classification.difficultyReason: Derive unlabelled heights using Pythagoras, express and combine the four supplied component areas and turn the strict geometric containment into a bound on π.

content.prompt: Approximate the area of this quarter circle by finding the sum of the areas of the four regions depicted below. Hence, show that $\pi>3$.

spec.description: Radius-two quarter circle containing a unit square, two congruent trapezia and a triangle. Internal lines terminate at the arc-intersection vertices. Alternating light orange and unfilled regions identify the four components; curved gaps remain visible.
spec.mathematics: Centre (0,0), radius 2; internal partitions x=1 and y=1. Inscribed boundary vertices are (0,2), (1,sqrt(3)), (sqrt(3),1), (2,0). Only the four source labels 1 are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: No derived lengths, component areas or numerical approximation are printed.

answer.short:
$3$ square units; $\pi>3$.

The four inscribed regions have total area $3$, strictly less than the quarter-circle area $\pi$.
answer.worked:
The radius is $2$. At the point on the arc above the unit square, let the height above the base be $h$.

$$\begin{align*} h^2&=2^2-1^2\\ h^2&=3\\ h&=\sqrt3. \end{align*}$$
The square has area $1$. Each trapezium has parallel sides $1$ and $\sqrt3-1$ and perpendicular height $1$. The remaining triangle has perpendicular sides $\sqrt3-1$.

$$\begin{align*} A_{\text{inscribed}}&=1+2\left(\frac{1+(\sqrt3-1)}{2}\right)+\frac{(\sqrt3-1)^2}{2}\\ A_{\text{inscribed}}&=1+\sqrt3+2-\sqrt3\\ A_{\text{inscribed}}&=3. \end{align*}$$
The quarter circle has area $\frac14\pi(2)^2=\pi$. It also contains the curved gaps outside the straight inscribed boundary, so its area is strictly greater than $3$. Therefore, $\pi>3$.
